chapters.title: Chapter 13: Better to Be Wanted by the Police Than Not to Be Wanted at All (Attacks against public figures)

assets.topic: Media-age mass behavior at the Paramount Theater
assets.visual_frame_description: A frozen newsreel frame from December 30, 1942: Frank Sinatra stands at the microphone on the stage of the Paramount Theater in New York while a crowd of bobby-soxed teenagers tears through the aisles, some climbing the stage, blouses and hair pulled apart. A reporter's typewriter beside the frame types the words 'mass frustrated love' and 'mass hypnosis' as the psychiatrists of the day struggle for an explanation. Two small insets on the wall show the same theater two years later with 30,000 fans and 450 police officers on duty.
assets.player_mission: Study the audience behavior in the frame and decide what fundamentally changed in the relationship between audiences and the famous. Identify the correct interpretation of the crowd's behavior so you can apply it to understanding modern public-figure risk.
assets.target_channel: Crowd emotional contagion: audience conduct, clothing and hair disturbance, boarding the stage, and the shift from contained admiration to personal pursuit
assets.question: Before the 1940s, a single woman shrieking through an entire show would have been taken to an asylum, yet on December 30, 1942 the entire Paramount audience screamed, tore at their clothes and hair, and left their seats to board the stage. What is the correct reading of this change in behavior?
assets.correct_cue: The cue is that a new contagious audience behavior appeared and became normalized within two years: the same acts that shocked everyone in 1942 were expected in 1944, when the 30,000 screaming fans and the 450 police officers were predicted and prepared for in advance. What changed is not individual madness but the media-age institutionalization of idolatry: love of public figures had been contained and distant, a one-way emotional street expressed only through acceptable functions like applauding, voting, letters, or seeing a show, and now audiences made themselves personally known to performers. The evidence of contagion is that the behavior spread, reporters learned to manipulate it to their advantage, and what surprised everyone in 1942 became routine by 1944 - the definition of the mass hypnosis the media age brought into American life.
distractors: The shrieking fans were individual cases of psychiatric disorder that emerged independently in the same theater that night.
Sinatra's singing style was later proven to have hypnotic properties, which is why the same crowd behavior has never recurred with any other performer.
Audience behavior remained constant across the decade; only the size of the crowd grew as national radio made Sinatra more popular.
assets.underlying_psychology: Mass hypnosis of the media age: behavior that was deviant became normalized once the media amplified it, and the emotional one-way street toward public figures became a two-way street in which fans pursued their idols. De Becker uses the 1942-1944 Paramount crowd to show that the conditions of fame changed permanently, normalizing pursuit behaviors that public-figure protection must now contend with.
key_concepts: On December 30, 1942, while Frank Sinatra sang at the Paramount Theater in New York, the behavior of the audience changed and a part of the relationship to well-known people changed forever.
Before the 1940s, an audience member who shrieked at the top of her lungs throughout an entire show would have been carted off to an asylum.
By the mid-forties, entire audiences screamed, tore at their clothes and hair, and left their seats to board the stage.
Psychiatrists and psychologists of the day explained the phenomenon as 'mass frustrated love' and 'mass hypnosis.'
Before the advent of mass media, love for performers was contained and emotionally distant, a one-way street displayed only through acceptable functions like voting, letters, and seeing a show.
In the Sinatra days, behavior that had been unacceptable, such as waiting hours outside a hotel to tear pieces of clothing from a passing star, became normal.
Two years after the 1942 Paramount appearance, the 30,000 screaming bobby-soxed fans were expected in advance and 450 police officers were assigned to that one theater.
The media were learning to manipulate this new audience behavior to their advantage.
The media age brought a type of mass hypnosis into American life that affects all of us to some degree and some of us to a great degree.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests mass behavioral contagion: media amplification converted previously deviant audience conduct into expected, normalized behavior within two years. De Becker's evidence is the 1942-1944 Paramount Theater crowd, which he uses to show the media age institutionalizing idolatry and normalizing pursuit of public figures.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.visual_frame_description: A threat-assessment desk on a film-studio lot in the 1980s. An open intake file shows a chronology of one subject's conduct: letters to an actress routed through her agent, a diary, a bus ticket, a gun purchase, and a trip to see the Dakota Building where John Lennon was murdered. A laminated card on the desk lists 'Ten Behaviors Common to Modern Assassins' with checkmarks beside nearly every item.
assets.player_mission: Read the intake file the way a Threat Assessment and Management analyst would. Decide which documented behaviors carry predictive weight and give the correct risk reading of the file.
assets.target_channel: Documented behavioral record over time: diary-keeping, weapon acquisition, travel patterns, communications with public figures, and identification with prior attackers
assets.question: A subject has displayed a mental disorder, created a diary, obtained a weapon, communicated inappropriately with a public figure, exhibited random crisscross travel, identified with a prior assassin, and made repeated approaches to public figures. What is the correct reading of the file?
assets.correct_cue: The correct reading is that the protocol of assassination is being followed: nearly every one of Park Dietz's ten behaviors common to modern assassins is present, and because assassins teach each other through documented methods, the process leaves an observable trail. The most decision-relevant cue is that this subject studied and identified with an earlier assassin and replicated his behaviors - the same pattern that linked Hinckley and Bardo, who matched on more than thirty striking similarities including carrying a copy of Catcher in the Rye - because identification with a prior assassin is itself one of Dietz's ten named behaviors. A diary is not a harmless prop but a named item on the list ('Created a diary, journal, or record'), and random travel plus repeated approaches are likewise named indicators.
distractors: Because a mental disorder was already displayed, the file is a psychiatric matter and the behaviors require no security response.
Because the subject wrote to a public figure other than the one who might be attacked, he poses no threat to anyone.
Diary-keeping and random travel are harmless fan habits with no weight in a risk assessment.
assets.underlying_psychology: Pre-incident indicators are detectable factors that occur before the outcome being predicted, and assassination is reached by a protocol of observable, detectable hoops that leave a trail. Dietz's ten behaviors, assembled from his pioneering work on threats and stalking, confirm that public-figure attack is a patterned, predictable process rather than a random act.
key_concepts: Park Dietz, the psychiatrist and sociologist who led the research project de Becker proposed on people who threaten and stalk public figures, assembled ten behaviors common to modern assassins.

Nearly every one of Dietz's ten behaviors is present in modern assassins: displayed some mental disorder, researched the target, created a diary or journal, obtained a weapon, communicated inappropriately with a public figure, displayed grandiosity, exhibited random travel, identified with a stalker or assassin, had the ability to circumvent ordinary security, and made repeated approaches to public figures.
En route to his crime, a would-be assassin communicated inappropriately with some public figure, though not necessarily the one attacked.
Dietz's list includes 'displayed an exaggerated idea of self (grandiosity, narcissism)' as a common behavior.
Assassins teach each other, each learning something from the ones before, which is why the process leaves a detectable trail.
John Hinckley and Robert Bardo shared more than thirty striking similarities in their pre-attack behavior.
Both Hinckley and Bardo brought a copy of Catcher in the Rye on their trips to attack, following the example of Mark Chapman, who carried it when he killed John Lennon.
Bardo told de Becker he read Catcher in the Rye 'to find out how it had made Chapman kill John Lennon.'
De Becker's office evaluates a hundred and fifty pre-incident indicators beyond the ten common behaviors in protecting public figures.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests detection of pre-incident indicators: assassins reach their crime by a protocol of observable, detectable hoops that leave a trail. Dietz's ten behaviors, plus the thirty-plus Hinckley-Bardo parallels, show that public-figure attack is a patterned, predictable process rather than a random act.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The bodyguard's unhonored intuition at the Citizen Tournament
assets.visual_frame_description: A Hamburg tennis stadium in 1993, frozen a second before impact: Monica Seles crouches at the service line while a thin spectator in the lower stands sways as he walks. A bodyguard in a suit holds a coffee cup and watches the man, a thought bubble above him reading 'Something told me that something was not quite right... I cannot explain it in more detail.'
assets.player_mission: Study the bodyguard's own channel: what his intuition registered, what he did with it, and why the moment was lost. Give the correct reading of his accurate-but-unhonored signal.
assets.target_channel: The observer's somatic intuition channel and the attacker's gait: swaying instead of walking, an unexplained uneasy feeling, and inaction despite the signal
assets.question: Bodyguard Henry reported: 'Call it a sixth sense or whatever, I cannot explain it, but I noticed the man. Something told me that something was not quite right with this man. He was swaying instead of walking.' What is the correct reading of this intuition?
assets.correct_cue: The correct reading is that Henry's intuition was accurate but unhonored: he pegged the attacker correctly and felt an uneasy signal before the stabbing, yet because he could not explain it he took no protective action - he put down the coffee cup he was holding even though he was on a protective detail for the most controversial figure in world tennis, strolled off to do something he himself did not know what, and the attack started and finished within a few steps. The cue that matters is not the swaying gait alone but the gap between a correct intuitive signal and zero protective action, which is why de Becker stresses that Henry's main message was that he 'cannot explain it in more detail' - the intuition was right and still produced nothing.
distractors: An intuition that cannot be verbally explained is by definition unreliable and was correctly ignored.
Henry's unease was a false alarm; the stabbing was a matter of timing coincidence, not something intuition could detect.
Because Henry noticed Parche earlier in the day at the player hotel, his duty was satisfied and the attack was unforeseeable.
assets.underlying_psychology: Intuition outruns explanation: the signal arrived, but the verbal justification did not, and the protective step was skipped. De Becker's point is not to criticize Henry and Manfred, who 'know not what they do' - that is exactly the point: they were unqualified part-timers, a telecommunications worker and a Hamburg harbor loader, put in charge of a star's life without a plan.
key_concepts: At the 1993 Citizen Tournament in Germany, Monica Seles was stabbed in the back by Gunter Parche and fell bleeding from a serious injury.
Amazingly, both Seles bodyguards reported that they took special notice of assailant Gunter Parche prior to the stabbing.
Bodyguard Henry pegged the attacker accurately: the man was swaying instead of walking, and something told Henry something was not quite right.
Henry's main message was that he could not explain his intuition in more detail.
Instead of acting, Henry put down the coffee cup he was holding even though he was on a protective detail and strolled over to do he didn't know what.
The attack had started and finished by the time Henry had taken only a few steps.
Seles's two bodyguards were unqualified part-timers: one a telecommunications worker with a side job at the private guard firm, the other a loader at Hamburg harbor.
The promoters did not tell Seles that the people they had assigned to guard her life were unqualified part-timers.
It is perhaps not fair to criticize Henry and Manfred, for they know not what they do; that, however, is exactly the point.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the gap between intuitive detection and protective action: Henry's somatic signal was accurate, yet he discounted it because he could not explain it, and the attack succeeded. De Becker's case evidence is the Seles security detail, where unqualified part-timers failed to convert an accurate 'sixth sense' into any protective step.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: Ability belief as the preeminent pre-incident indicator
assets.visual_frame_description: An analyst's whiteboard in a security office: one column lists the 150 pre-incident indicators the office evaluates, with a single line highlighted in yellow reading 'ABILITY BELIEF.' Beside it hangs a small sketch of a diver leaping from a two-hundred-foot Acapulco cliff into the Pacific, and on the right edge a timeline shows public-figure attacks clustered in pairs.
assets.player_mission: Identify the single most predictive pre-incident indicator and understand how it is raised and lowered. Choose the correct reading of the evidence on the board.
assets.target_channel: The subject's own capability self-assessment: stated and behavioral evidence of whether he believes he can complete a public-figure attack
assets.question: Across the 150 pre-incident indicators de Becker's office evaluates, which single PIN does he call the one he would want to be aware of above all others, and why?
assets.correct_cue: The correct cue is ability belief - the person's belief that he can accomplish a public-figure attack - because without it, he cannot: to do anything, each of us must first believe on some level that we can do it, and if the truthful answer is 'No, what with all those Secret Service agents and special arrangements, I couldn't get within a mile of the guy,' the person cannot shoot the president. The evidence for why it is the preeminent PIN is that it is the hinge the other indicators turn on and it is mutable: it is influenced by encouragement, by teaching the component skills of the act, by taking lesser steps first, and most powerfully by social proof - seeing someone else succeed at the thing you believed you could not do. That is why attacks cluster after wide publicity: President Ford was attacked twice within two weeks and President Clinton twice within six weeks, because the coverage says 'You see; it can be done.'
distractors: The strongest PIN is the number of death threats the subject has made toward public figures.
The strongest PIN is weapon acquisition, because possessing a weapon equals capability.
The strongest PIN is a diagnosed mental disorder, because nearly every assassin displays one.
assets.underlying_psychology: Self-efficacy belief is the gatekeeper of action: the would-be attacker cannot begin what he does not believe possible, and that belief is socially contagious. De Becker's evidence is the cliff-dive analogy and the observed clustering of attacks after highly publicized ones, which he attributes to media-supported ability belief.
key_concepts: De Becker's office evaluates a hundred and fifty pre-incident indicators in each case beyond the ten common behaviors.
If we had to choose just one pre-incident indicator to be aware of above all others, it would be the one called ability belief.
Ability belief is a person's belief that he can accomplish a public-figure attack; without it, he cannot.
To do anything, each of us must first believe on some level that we can do it.
Ability belief is not a permanently reliable predictor, because it can be influenced and changed.
No single influence on ability belief is more powerful than social proof: seeing someone else succeed at the thing you might have initially believed you could not do.
Seeing a diver propel himself off an Acapulco cliff, sail down into the Pacific, and emerge safely dramatically influences the belief that it can be done, and that the observer could do it.
The enormous media attention showered on those who attack public figures bolsters ability belief in others; it says, 'You see; it can be done.'
In the period following a widely publicized attack, the risk of other attacks goes up dramatically: President Ford was attacked twice within two weeks and President Clinton twice within six weeks.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests ability belief as the preeminent pre-incident indicator: without the belief that an attack can succeed, the attack cannot occur. De Becker's evidence is comparative case experience plus the social-proof mechanism, which he links to the observed two-within-two-weeks and two-within-six-weeks clustering of attacks after heavy publicity.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.topic: The lovesick-fan mislabel at the studio gate
assets.visual_frame_description: A sunny morning at a Hollywood studio gate where a sitcom is taped. A wiry young man in a windbreaker stands before a security chief's booth; a cross-country bus idles in the background and a map on the wall shows the route from Tucson, Arizona. In the chief's hand is a clipboard, and his headset log reads 'Fan number ninety-four this year - standard procedure.'
assets.player_mission: Review the encounter the way the security team should have. Catch the warning signs in the interaction and select the correct reading before the file closes.
assets.target_channel: The pursuer's conduct in the single encounter: mode and distance of travel, insistency of language, fixation on the celebrity's name, and the observer's own acknowledgment that something was wrong
assets.question: Robert Bardo, who had sent Rebecca Schaeffer a stream of inappropriate letters over two years, traveled from Arizona by bus and told the studio's security chief he was in love with the actress. The chief refused him entry and drove him back to his motel. What is the correct reading of this encounter?
assets.correct_cue: The correct reading is that obvious warning signs were present and unrecognized: obsessive letter volume routed through her agents in New York and Los Angeles for two years, a cross-country bus trip by a man with no ties to the city, and an insistence so intense that 'Rebecca Schaeffer' was every other word - 'I gotta see her. I love her.' - that the chief himself described as 'something was definitely wrong mentally... something was haywire going on.' The decisive missing step is that nobody informed Rebecca Schaeffer the pursuer existed, and Bardo's own verdict on the whole system was 'It was way too easy.'
distractors: Because Bardo never threatened the actress and left when refused, no warning signs existed in the encounter.
Handling Bardo as one of the hundred fan attempts the studio sees in a year was the correct standard procedure.
The chief's ride to the motel ended the risk, because Bardo had been personally warned and driven away.
assets.underlying_psychology: Denial through mislabeling: when an escalating pursuer is filed under 'just lovesick,' each observed indicator loses its weight and no action follows. De Becker's case evidence is the Schaeffer studio chief, who saw the signs, did not perceive them as potentially violent, and later asked 'What more could I have done?'
key_concepts: Over a two-year period, Robert Bardo sent Rebecca Schaeffer a stream of inappropriate letters through her agents in New York and Los Angeles.
When Bardo showed up at the studio where her show was taped, it was a studio security guard who told him which stage she was on.
Bardo himself said of gaining access, 'It was way too easy.'
Bardo told the chief of security that he was in love with Rebecca Schaeffer and had traveled from Arizona to see her.
The security chief did not see to it that Rebecca Schaeffer was informed about the man who had been pursuing her for two years and had just traveled hundreds of miles by bus to meet her.
The chief said of Bardo: 'Rebecca Schaeffer' was every other word, 'I gotta see her. I love her. Something was definitely wrong mentally. There was something haywire going on.'
The chief explained, 'I thought he was just lovesick. We get a hundred in a year, people trying to get in, fans writing letters.'
To the security chief it was a matter of handling a fan according to standard procedure, but to Bardo it was a powerful and emotional event.
Bardo transferred the extreme anger he felt toward the studio security onto Ms. Schaeffer: he perceived her as the one who said he was not wanted.
The chief's unanswered refrain two weeks after the murder: 'What more could I have done?'
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the mislabeling form of denial: fitting an escalating pursuer into the benign category of 'lovesick fan' so that standard procedure replaces risk action. De Becker's case evidence is the Schaeffer studio chief, who saw several obvious warning signs, acknowledged something was haywire, and still did not inform the target.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.visual_frame_description: A 1949 hotel corridor at the Edgewater Beach Hotel in Chicago: an open door to room 1297-A, a suitcase of baseball memorabilia on the floor, and a crumpled letter in a trash can; a hotel card on the door reads 'Do Not Disturb.' Insets show a pawnshop receipt for a rifle and a ringing lobby telephone, with a newspaper headline about the shooting of first baseman Eddie Waitkus.
assets.player_mission: Audit the subject's file: weigh her baseline, her timed actions, and her recorded statements against her story of unrequited love. Deliver the correct diagnosis of what actually drove the shooting.
assets.question: On the morning of June 14, 1949, nineteen-year-old Ruth Steinhagen shot Chicago Cubs first baseman Eddie Waitkus in his hotel room and told police her dreams had come true. Audit her statements and behavior: was this crime driven by unrequited romantic love?
assets.subject_baseline: A devoted fan of Eddie Waitkus who set an empty chair facing hers at dinner each evening because 'Eddie is in that chair,' learned Lithuanian because he was of Lithuanian descent, collected everything tied to his jersey number 36, slept with his picture under her pillow, sent letter after letter he never answered, and attended every game she could while her parents grew concerned enough to take her to two psychiatrists.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: June 13, 1949, evening: tells her friend Joyce to 'watch for the fireworks on Tuesday.' June 14, 1949: 9:30 AM checks into the Edgewater Beach Hotel in Chicago carrying a suitcase of Eddie memorabilia, including ticket stubs from fifty games she had attended, plus a rifle bought at a pawnshop after a pistol permit was denied; 11:00 AM writes a farewell note to her parents ('I hope you understand things. I love you.'), then crumples it and throws it in the trash; 11:45 AM writes a polite, businesslike note to Waitkus signed 'Ruth Anne Burns' and tips a bellman three dollars to deliver it; 1:30 PM places a knife in her skirt pocket intending to stab him in the heart as he enters, then retrieves the rifle from the closet; 2:00 PM fires one shot into his chest. After the shooting she is 'burning because nobody was coming out of those other rooms. Nobody seemed to want me much. I could've walked right out of that place and nobody would have come after me.'
assets.interrogation_transcript: Ruth: 'I liked him a great deal and knew I could never have him, and if I couldn't have him neither could anybody else.' / Ruth: 'I've always wanted to be in the limelight. I wanted attention and publicity for once. My dreams have come true.' / Ruth, describing the aftermath: 'I got mad. I kept telling them I shot Eddie Waitkus, but they didn't know who Eddie Waitkus was.' / Ruth's mother, earlier, when Ruth announced her intention: 'You can't do that. Women don't do those things.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: The motive was identity-seeking, not romance: Ruth wanted attention and publicity - she stated it plainly - and the emotional logic of the crime was 'better to be wanted by the police than not to be wanted at all.' Her distress after shooting Waitkus was that no one in the hotel came out to see her, not remorse over the act.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: 1) The planning contradicts the heartbreak story: a polite decoy note, a knife chosen first, a rifle chosen because a pistol required a permit, and a suitcase of fifty ticket stubs show logistics and staging, not a lovers' quarrel. 2) Her own words supply the motive: 'I wanted attention and publicity for once. My dreams have come true.' 3) The crumpled farewell letter shows a suicide plan that was replaced by something better: an attack that would make her famous, which is the same 'attention-getting suicide' pattern on John Hinckley's pre-attack list. 4) Her complaint about the aftermath - nobody wanted her, she could have walked out - reveals the true reward she sought: to be the object of attention, even police attention.
distractors: She was a spurned lover driven temporarily insane by Waitkus's trade to the Philadelphia Phillies and his failure to answer her letters.
She intended to die with him, so the shooting was an attempted murder-suicide that the ambulance interrupted.
Her delusion that Eddie occupied the empty chair at dinner proves psychosis alone, and any understandable motive, explains the attack.
key_concepts: Ruth Steinhagen devoted her life to Eddie Waitkus even though they had never met, and 'Eddie is in that chair' was her explanation of an empty chair at the dinner table.
When Waitkus was traded to the Philadelphia Phillies, Ruth stated that she could not live if he moved away from Chicago.
She wanted a pistol, but because a permit was required she went to a pawnshop and bought a rifle instead.
Ruth brought a suitcase filled with Eddie memorabilia to the hotel, including the ticket stubs from fifty games she had attended.
She told police, 'I've always wanted to be in the limelight. I wanted attention and publicity for once. My dreams have come true.'
Ruth's lasting anger after the shooting was that nobody came out of their rooms and nobody seemed to want her much.
Valerie Solanas, who shot Andy Warhol, told a Times Square cop, 'The police are looking for me... They want me.'
Ruth's mother said, 'You can't do that. Women don't do those things' - a prediction disproved by Ruth, Valerie Solanas, Squeaky Fromme, and Sara Jane Moore.
Ruth Steinhagen became the first in a long line of media-age public-figure stalkers and attackers, 'the senior member of a uniquely American minority.'
People who do not get a feeling of significance in childhood seek ways to get it in adulthood, as if malnourished for a lifetime and seeking to fix it with one huge meal.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests identity-seeking motivation: people who do not get a feeling of significance in childhood seek it in adulthood, and an attack can serve as a single huge meal of significance. De Becker's case evidence is Ruth Steinhagen and Valerie Solanas, who sought fame through their attacks and preferred police attention to none at all.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.visual_frame_description: A small concrete prison cell with two benches anchored to the floor and, beyond the door, a long green corridor ending at a locked steel gate. A young man with light stubble and a mess of prematurely receding hair sits with his head down; a tape recorder rests on the bench between the two men, and a guard's silhouette stands behind the gate window.
assets.player_mission: Run the interview the way it was run: let him speak first, follow rather than lead, and audit his self-presentation against the case facts. Deliver the correct diagnosis of what Bardo is really doing.
assets.question: In your cell interview, Robert Bardo opens by relaying a message from Arthur Jackson and offers to 'help other people avoid what happened to Rebecca.' Audit his self-presentation against the facts. What is he really doing?
assets.subject_baseline: An awkward, teenage-looking man with light stubble and prematurely receding hair - 'a geek' by his own account - who never had friends and never had a romantic kiss; an apprentice assassin who corresponded with Mark Chapman to ask why he killed John Lennon, hired a private detective because Arthur Jackson had used one, and carried a knife on an earlier trip to kill Schaeffer because Jackson had used a knife.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-15:00: sits with his head down in the locked cell, silent, reluctant to make eye contact, as de Becker waits him out without a single question; 15:30: finally looks up and studies de Becker's face intently before speaking; throughout: grows animated whenever the subject is his public image, how he 'stacks up' against other assassins, or the fame his act achieved; posture and tone shift when he says the media portray him 'in ways I never saw myself.'
assets.interrogation_transcript: Bardo: 'Arthur Jackson asked me to give you a message. He wants you to meet with him too.' / de Becker: 'Not today.' / Bardo: 'Then why do you want to talk to me?' / de Becker: 'Because you have something to contribute.' / Bardo: 'I do want to help other people avoid what happened to Rebecca.' / de Becker: 'Nothing just happened to Rebecca. You make it seem as if she had an accident.' / Bardo: 'No, no. I killed her. I shot her, and I want to help others not get killed by someone like me.' / de Becker: 'That sounds like you think there is someone else like you.' / Bardo: 'There is. I mean there are... many people like me.' / Bardo: 'I'm not a monster. On television they always want to portray me as someone frightening.' / Bardo: 'That video of me telling how I shot Rebecca makes me look like the worst assassin of all, and I'm not the worst.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Self-serving image management built on a minimized-agency framing: his volunteered offer casts the killing as something that 'happened to' Rebecca - de Becker heard the passive construction as claiming 'some distance from his crime' and refused to grant it. Bardo is auditioning to become 'the anti-assassin,' distinguishing himself from other assassins and controlling how his story is recorded; his concern throughout is his public image and his rank among killers, not the victim.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: 1) Framing test: 'What happened to Rebecca' versus 'I killed her. I shot her.' When challenged, he concedes the facts but immediately re-offers the redemption story, which shows the frame matters more to him than the correction. 2) His stated reason for talking is not remorse but contribution: 'you have something to contribute' is what engages him. 3) Serial concern for image: he wants to avoid being 'the worst,' argues the television portrayal is unfair, and says the media 'portray me in ways I never saw myself.' 4) The every-assassin echo: 'there are... many people like me' - even his confession converts the crime into membership in a category he ranks within. 5) His famous advice to celebrities - 'Be careful about what you write... don't let it be so over-glowing' - shows he still reads the relationship through his obsession, in which Rebecca's kind postcard 'propelled' him to want more.
distractors: Bardo is telling the truth: he genuinely wants to prevent other attacks and has fully accepted responsibility for his crime.
Bardo is working as an informant and is using the interview to arrange a meeting with Arthur Jackson.
Bardo's quiet, submissive demeanor proves he regrets the murder and is no longer any threat to anyone.
key_concepts: Bardo had studied those who came before him, writing to Mark Chapman after the killing of John Lennon to ask why he had done it.
Bardo told de Becker that if Chapman had advised against his crime, 'that would not have overridden my emotions. Emotions are the key, out-of-balance emotions.'
The greatest intimacy most assassins attain is with those they attack: through stalking they come to know their victims more closely than they know others in their lives.
For assassins, it is the act and not the target, the destination and not the journey, that matters; Bardo stalked several famous people, giving up on one client of de Becker's as too inaccessible.
Bardo expected exactly what he got - an unenthusiastic reception and ultimately rejection - and used that rejection as an excuse for his terrible anger.
A lack of healthy intimacy is a common feature of many assassins: neither Hinckley, Jackson, nor Bremer attained a developed romantic relationship.
Rebecca Schaeffer's only positive attention to Bardo - a postcard saying his letter was 'the nicest, most real letter I ever received' - is what propelled him to want more from her.
Bardo's advice to famous people was to be careful what they write and not to be so over-glowing to fans, because it makes fans feel they are the only one.
Bardo saw himself becoming 'the anti-assassin,' the assassin who helps famous people avoid danger.
Bardo noted a convoluted irony: 'All the fame that I have achieved from this results in me getting death threats and harassment... They portray me in ways I never saw myself.'
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests impression management in an identity-seeking offender: Bardo's narrative converts his murder into a credential that lets him be 'a peer' with celebrities, and he manages every exchange to control that image. De Becker's case evidence is the full prison interview, in which Bardo's offer to help reveals a continuing need to be significant rather than responsibility toward Rebecca Schaeffer.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.visual_frame_description: A CNN interview set in 1993: a promoter in a blazer gestures dismissively from a chair while a freeze-frame behind him shows a stadium gate where a spectator hands a ticket to an attendant and an unused metal-detector arch stands to the side. A caption card reads 'Metal detectors: ludicrous.'
assets.player_mission: Audit the promoter's claim line by line against the tournament's own logistics and his own career-long behavior. Deliver the correct diagnosis of his security argument.
assets.question: After Monica Seles was stabbed at the 1993 Citizen Tournament, tennis promoter Jerry Diamond told CNN that weapons screening with metal detectors could never work in tennis. Audit his claim against the tournament's own logistics. What is really going on?
assets.subject_baseline: A tournament promoter who says of the attack, 'it cost us as promoters a tremendous amount of revenue, so we selfishly try to make our security first-rate,' and who dismisses weapons screening at tennis as 'ludicrous' while describing himself as having 'first-rate' security.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: CNN interview: opens with a dismissive gesture when weapons screening is mentioned; leans back expansively while explaining the roof-and-walls argument; voice sharpens on the word 'ludicrous'; produces no data on any attempted screening anywhere in tennis; grows animated and apologetic when discussing revenue lost after the attack; visibly relaxes when returning to the claim that such attacks cannot be prevented.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Diamond: 'When you are working in an enclosed facility where you've got walls and a ceiling and a roof, yeah, all those things are possible. But a metal detector is not going to deter anyone who is determined to go in that direction.' / Diamond: 'When [Seles] got stabbed in Germany, it cost us as promoters a tremendous amount of revenue, so we selfishly try to make our security first-rate.' / Diamond, on weapons screening: 'ludicrous.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Motivated reasoning presented as technical expertise: the claim that screening cannot work because some facilities lack roofs is a rationalization built to reach a pre-chosen conclusion - that the attack was unpreventable, which relieves promoters of any duty to prevent it. His own career refutes him: throughout his career he has 'managed to screen every single spectator for something far smaller than a weapon: a tiny piece of paper, the ticket he sold them.'
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: 1) False premise: weapons screening works where there is no ceiling - the Super Bowl has none - and courthouses, airlines, TV-show audiences, city halls, concerts, and high schools all screen as routine; Parche at the Citizen Tournament and Bardo at Schaeffer's TV taping both reached their targets armed while audiences were uninspected. 2) Self-interest is stated aloud: revenue was lost, so prevention is made to look impossible; if attacks are unpreventable, then he and other promoters have no duty to try to prevent them. 3) The standardization excuse fails on the record: tennis already standardizes ball bounce height (135 to 147 centimeters from 2.5 meters) and court dimensions (23.8 meters long, 8.2 meters wide) worldwide, so a standard credential and access-control system is plainly possible. 4) The function of the argument is to move the attack into the category of fate - precisely the fatalism de Becker says people apply to their own safety as an excuse not to take reasonable precautions.
distractors: Diamond is factually correct that metal detectors are physically incapable of operating in open-air venues, so tennis genuinely cannot use them.
Diamond's point is spectator privacy: fans have a right to enter a sports venue without being searched.
Diamond is honestly reporting that no security existed at the tournament, so nothing could have been done.
key_concepts: Promoter Jerry Diamond told CNN that weapons screening would never work in tennis because 'a metal detector is not going to deter anyone who is determined to go in that direction.'
Diamond said the stabbing 'cost us as promoters a tremendous amount of revenue, so we selfishly try to make our security first-rate.'
Diamond has managed to screen every single spectator for something far smaller than a weapon: a tiny piece of paper, the ticket he sold them.
Weapons screening is good enough for courthouses, airlines, TV shows, city halls, concerts, high schools, and even the Super Bowl, which has no ceiling.

Most television shows now have metal-detector screening for audiences, because armed people with intent could otherwise reach a TV star, as Robert Bardo did carrying a concealed knife and as Parche did at the Citizen Tournament.

Everywhere in the world, tennis requires that each ball bounce 135 to 147 centimeters when dropped from 2.5 meters, and courts must be exactly 23.8 meters by 8.2 meters - so standardization of security is possible.
If attacks are unpreventable, then promoters have no duty to try to prevent them, which is what makes the fatalistic argument convenient.

Weak security improvements - including those you might make in your own life - are sometimes worse than doing nothing, because they give false peace of mind and convince people that safety is being addressed when it is not.
The knife attack is the most preventable of all assassination methods.

After the attack, the Women's Tennis Council publicized enhanced security yet did not require promoters to use metal detectors for screening spectators or to install clear plastic audience barricades like those at hockey games.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests denial dressed as expertise: fatalism applied to prevention, the claim that violence cannot be prevented, is used as an excuse to take no precautions and is delivered with misplaced confidence. De Becker's evidence is the Seles aftermath, in which promoters argued weapons screening was impossible while routinely screening every spectator for a ticket every day of their careers.

assets.visual_frame_description: A prison interview room from the viewpoint of the man at the call button: across the table looms a six-foot-nine giant, and as guards enter, one enormous hand rests on the interviewer's shoulder while the giant grins. A wall clock shows thirty minutes elapsed and a tape-recorder reel is still turning.
assets.player_mission: Review the locked-cell encounter between agent Robert Ressler and Edmund Kemper: weigh the timing, the contradictions, and the performance. Deliver the correct diagnosis of Kemper's final 'just kidding' line.
assets.question: Locked in a cell with FBI agent Robert Ressler, Edmund Kemper spends thirty minutes holding him in a contest of fear and courage, then says as he is walked out: 'You know I was just kidding, don't you?' Audit this denial. What is really happening?
assets.subject_baseline: A six-foot-nine, three-hundred-plus-pound killer of ten people, several of whom he had decapitated, serving seven life terms; a man who has endured a long abstinence from his compulsive habit of murder and, in the cell, now had a live one: a famous FBI agent.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: Ressler presses the call button three times over about fifteen minutes with no guard responding; Kemper watches him and calmly explains the shift change and the fifteen-to-twenty-minute delay; he leans forward to describe how he could screw Ressler's head off and place it on the table to greet the guard; he scoffs at the threat of federal prosecution; he wins a thirty-minute contest of fear and courage, deflecting every one of Ressler's behavioral gambits; as he is walked out he places one enormous hand on Ressler's shoulder and delivers the 'just kidding' line.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Ressler: 'You don't seriously think I'd come in here without some way to defend myself, do you?' / Kemper: 'They don't let anybody bring guns in here.' / Ressler: 'FBI agents have special privileges. A gun might not be the only weapon available to me.' / Kemper: 'What have you got, a poison pen?' / Kemper, of killing a federal official: 'What would they do, cut off my TV privileges?' / Kemper, earlier: 'If I went apeshit in here, you'd be in a lot of trouble. I could screw your head off and place it on the table to greet the guard.' / Kemper, as he is walked out: 'You know I was just kidding, don't you?'
assets.correct_diagnosis: False reassurance deployed at the moment the threat phase ended: the 'just kidding' reframe rewrites a deliberate, enjoyed dominance performance as play. Kemper had accurately priced the murder - time in the hole and lost TV privileges were 'a small price to pay for the prestige of offing an FBI agent' - had calculated that Ressler did not stand a chance against his size and experience, and had been feeding on a favorite delicacy of serial killers: human fear. The denial lets him keep the experience and the alibi simultaneously.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: 1) Timing: the reassurance never comes while the door is locked; it comes only when guards arrive and he is walked out - the denial is for the record, not a genuine correction. 2) Contradiction: minutes earlier he had negotiated the cost-benefit of the murder, calling it a small price to pay for prestige, and had mocked Ressler's only defense with 'What have you got, a poison pen?' so the 'kidding' claim contradicts his own stated calculus. 3) Function: recasting lethal threats as jokes lets him harvest the fear he induced while maintaining a friendly veneer for the officials who will write the reports. 4) The verdict, as conveyed to de Becker by Ressler, is unambiguous: Kemper was not just kidding.
distractors: Kemper was cooperative: his calm explanation of the guard shift change shows he was helping Ressler manage the situation.
Kemper's threats were idle ruminations he had genuinely abandoned once Ressler threatened federal consequences.
Ressler's bluff about a concealed weapon is what actually deterred Kemper from attacking.
key_concepts: Edmund Kemper, who had brutally killed ten people, several of whom he had decapitated, was six foot nine inches tall and more than three hundred pounds.
Kemper had endured a long abstinence from his compulsive habit of murder and now had a live one: a famous FBI agent.
Kemper told Ressler, 'If I went apeshit in here, you'd be in a lot of trouble. I could screw your head off and place it on the table to greet the guard.'
Against Kemper's terrific size advantage and experience at killing, Ressler did not stand a chance.
Kemper called time in the hole 'a small price to pay for the prestige of offing an FBI agent.'
When Ressler said he would be in big trouble for murdering a federal official, Kemper scoffed, 'What would they do, cut off my TV privileges?'
There followed a thirty-minute contest of fear and courage, with Ressler using his behavioral insight to keep Kemper off balance.

Ressler's gambit, 'You don't seriously think I'd come in here without some way to defend myself, do you?' drew the answer, 'They don't let anybody bring guns in here,' and Kemper added, 'What have you got, a poison pen?'
As Kemper was walked out, he put one of his enormous hands on Ressler's shoulder and said, 'You know I was just kidding, don't you?'
Kemper was not just kidding: he was feeding on a favorite delicacy of serial killers: human fear.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests retrospective denial in a predator: Kemper turns a deliberate fear-feeding performance into 'just kidding' only after the threat window closes, preserving both the experience and a deniable account. De Becker's evidence is Ressler's account of the cell interview, an observational case report rather than an experiment.

assets.topic: Auditing the studio chief's 'What more could I have done?'
assets.visual_frame_description: A press scrum outside a studio gate days after the murder: a security chief in a gray uniform stands behind a microphone with hands raised slightly, while news captions repeat his phrase 'standard procedure.' Inset photographs show the same gate months earlier, with a cross-country bus arriving and a young man standing at the booth.
assets.player_mission: Audit the chief's public account against what he actually observed that day and what was actually done. Deliver the correct diagnosis of how the encounter was handled.
assets.question: After Rebecca Schaeffer's murder, the studio security chief who had met Robert Bardo explained the meeting to reporters. Audit his account: was the encounter handled as well as he says?
assets.subject_baseline: An experienced studio security chief who fields fan attempts regularly - 'We get a hundred in a year, people trying to get in, fans writing letters' - and runs encounters by what he calls standard procedure; he personally drove Bardo back to his motel after refusing him entry at the studio gate.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: During the interview he reaches for 'standard procedure' repeatedly as a framing device; he describes Bardo's insistence with specific, vivid recall ('Rebecca Schaeffer' was every other word); he volunteers unprompted that 'something was definitely wrong mentally'; after listing the warning signs he stops, pauses, and shifts to 'but I didn't perceive it as potentially violent'; he closes by asking a rhetorical question and looking away.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Chief: 'I thought he was just lovesick. We get a hundred in a year, people trying to get in, fans writing letters.' / Chief: 'Terribly insistent on being let in. Rebecca Schaeffer was every other word. I gotta see her. I love her. Something was definitely wrong mentally. There was something haywire going on, but I didn't perceive it as potentially violent.' / Chief: 'What more could I have done?'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Denial operating through a mislabel that excused inaction: the chief recognized several obvious warning signs - obsessive fixation, a two-year letter stream through the actress's agents, a cross-country bus trip, insistence he himself called haywire - yet filed the man under 'lovesick,' the routine category, and took none of the obvious protective steps: Rebecca Schaeffer was not even informed that the man existed. The closing rhetorical question converts an unperformed duty into fate.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: 1) Recognition is on the record: he observed that something was definitely wrong mentally and haywire, which is the moment a warning sign becomes a cue requiring a response. 2) The mislabel does the work: 'just lovesick' compresses the data - two years of letters, hundreds of miles of travel, refusal to leave - into a benign fan type that standard procedure already knows how to handle. 3) The cost is specific: he did not see to it that Rebecca Schaeffer was informed about the man who had been pursuing her for two years and had just traveled hundreds of miles by bus to meet her; the Janoff case two weeks later showed how differently outcomes run when the target is informed and prepared. 4) The rhetorical closing reframe, 'What more could I have done?' is the denial's signature: it asks the question as if the answer were obviously nothing. Bardo's own verdict on the overall system: 'It was way too easy.'
distractors: The chief was correct that Bardo was harmless, because Bardo made no threats in his presence.
The chief did everything possible: he refused Bardo entry, drove him to his motel, and the two never met again before the murder.
The chief lacked authority to act, since informing an actress about a fan was outside the studio security role.
key_concepts: In the Bardo case there were many warnings: over a two-year period he had sent Rebecca Schaeffer a stream of inappropriate letters through her agents in New York and Los Angeles.
The security chief did not see to it that Rebecca Schaeffer was informed about the 'lovesick' man who had been pursuing her for two years and had just traveled hundreds of miles by bus to meet her.
The chief said, 'I thought he was just lovesick. We get a hundred in a year, people trying to get in, fans writing letters.'
The chief acknowledged, 'Something was definitely wrong mentally. There was something haywire going on, but I didn't perceive it as potentially violent.'
To the security chief it was a matter of handling some fan according to what he called standard procedure, but to Bardo it was a powerful and emotional event.
Bardo said of the security team's rejection: 'I had problems with the security at the studio and the feeling I had toward them, I just put it on Ms. Schaeffer.'
The chief's unanswered refrain, repeated often after preventable tragedies: 'What more could I have done?'
About two weeks after Rebecca Schaeffer was killed, the Steven Janoff case showed that informing and preparing the target changes outcomes.
After the killing, several theatrical agencies, movie studios, and management firms began having inappropriate communications and visits professionally evaluated.
Media figures are now more likely to be informed of inappropriate pursuit, and successful attacks against media figures have been sharply reduced in recent years.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests denial as the enemy of prediction: recognized warning signs are neutralized by a benign label, and inaction is then reframed as fate. De Becker's case evidence is the Schaeffer studio chief, who saw the signs, acknowledged something haywire, and still never informed the target - followed by the unanswered refrain, 'What more could I have done?'

assets.topic: Full threat-assessment arc: the reasserting pursuer
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen of a theater district at dusk: on the left, the actress rehearses on stage with a changed entrance route and a security man in the wings; on the right, a log sheet of five days of sightings marked 'no encounter,' ending in a final frame of a man being led from a box office by police after a standoff.
assets.player_mission: Run the full protection arc: read the situation correctly, then choose the package of precautions that converts the threat into a controlled outcome. Select the correct risk reading in stage one and the correct intervention package in stage two.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests whether the player can turn pre-incident indicators into protective action: the lesson of the Steven Janoff case, in which detection plus a coordinated action plan stopped an armed pursuer, and the counter-lesson of the Seles case, in which unqualified security and no plan guaranteed the attack succeeded. The central claim being tested is that assassination and stalking violence are prevented far more often than they succeed, but only when warning signs are converted into action.
assets.stage_1_observation: A rehearsal theater in a city at dusk. An actress who once appeared in a client's television show stops mid-scene: through the stage door she has just seen a man outside the theater - the same man she was warned about a year ago, the pursuer called Steven Janoff. She calls the threat-assessment office, shaken. You open the file: Janoff previously pursued a client of the office; the evaluation judged him not likely a hazard to that client but potentially dangerous to this actress; police and studio security warned him off, assuming that would resolve the matter. It did not. The new log shows a man matching his description outside the theater twice this week.
assets.stage_1_question: Given the year of warnings, the failed police caution, and the fresh sightings, what is the correct reading of Janoff's risk level and the right posture for the actress and her team?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Elevated risk requiring a full precaution plan now. Janoff was already warned off once and returned anyway, so warnings alone do not resolve pursuit; the correct posture is to treat him as active and approaching. The evidence: after the threat was reported, the actress and her representatives asked for and exactly followed the recommendations, and despite five days of stalking, Janoff never once encountered her - proof that detection plus a coordinated plan defeats a determined pursuer until the authorities can remove him.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You now direct the actress's protective changes for the run of her play. Which package of actions matches the plan that actually worked in the Janoff case about two weeks after Rebecca Schaeffer's death?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The package that worked: she stopped using the front entrance of the theater for her rehearsal visits; the box office was provided with Janoff's photo and guidance on what to do if he showed up; she agreed to have a security person with her; and she applied several other strategies designed to limit the likelihood of an unwanted encounter. The result: for five days Janoff stalked her without an encounter, and when he finally walked up to the box office demanding to see her, an employee recognized him and sent out a call to police; after a four-hour standoff Janoff was taken into custody, his gun confirmed loaded, with a collection of other firearms back at his hotel room. The contrasting failure mode is the Seles tournament, where weak security improvements gave false peace of mind and convinced people safety was being addressed when it was not.
key_concepts: About two weeks after Rebecca Schaeffer was killed, the Steven Janoff case showed that informing and preparing the target changes outcomes.

A year before the incidents, Janoff had pursued a client of de Becker's office, and the evaluation determined he did not likely pose a hazard to that client but might be dangerous to a co-star on the client's television show.
The actress and her representatives were told about the case, and police and studio security warned the pursuer off, assuming that would resolve the matter.

The actress saw a man outside the theater who caught her attention, could not shake the feeling that he might be the person she had been warned about, and called the office; inquiry confirmed the man was Steven Janoff, in pursuit of her.

The actress and her representatives asked for and exactly followed the recommendations: she stopped using the front entrance, the box office got his photo and guidance, she had a security person with her, and she applied several other strategies.
For five days Janoff stalked the actress, but because of her precautions he was unable to encounter her.
Janoff bought a ticket for opening night but was not patient enough to wait; he walked to the box office, where an employee recognized him and called police.

Janoff produced a handgun and demanded to see the actress; after a four-hour standoff with police he was taken into custody, and not only was the gun loaded but he had a collection of other firearms at his hotel room.

The Janoff case shows the enormous improvements the entertainment industry has made: media figures are now more likely to be informed of inappropriate pursuit, and successful attacks against media figures have been sharply reduced in recent years.

People who apply a fatalistic attitude to their own safety, such as the claim that burglary cannot be prevented, do so as an excuse not to take reasonable precautions; the absence of precautions makes you vulnerable to the uncommitted criminal.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the full chain from pre-incident indicator to protective action: warnings only work when they change the target's behavior. De Becker's evidence pair is the Janoff case, where precautions produced zero encounters and a successful arrest, versus the Schaeffer and Seles cases, where no notification and unqualified guards made the attack 'way too easy.'

assets.topic: The press-conference battle: framing a captured attacker
assets.visual_frame_description: A federal press-briefing room: two draft press releases lie on the table, Draft A illustrated with handguns and ammunition laid on a hotel bureau, Draft B with a handcuffed man in a mangy T-shirt watched by a single guard in a gloomy corridor. Behind the podium, a wall screen shows the arrest staging of Timothy McVeigh and a magazine cover of Ted Kaczynski.
assets.player_mission: Choose the security-correct framing for the capture: spot the glamorizing elements, then rebuild the briefing so it deflates rather than advertises the crime. Select the correct reading in stage one and the correct presentation package in stage two.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests the advertising effect of media coverage: how the presentation of a captured attacker can either promote or deflate the fantasy that drives public-figure attack. The mechanism is social proof - the same influence that makes attacks cluster after publicity - so the way agencies frame an apprehension is a security decision, not just a public-relations one.
assets.stage_1_observation: A federal press-briefing room with cameras ready. You are the agent preparing the public statement after the arrest of a man who was planning to attack a public figure. On the table are two drafts: Draft A describes 'three .45-caliber handguns and more than two hundred rounds of ammunition in his hotel room. Since the perpetrator is a skilled marksman, it was touch and go when we stormed the building.' Draft B describes the same arrest as 'a twenty-two-year-old found hiding in the clothes hamper of the bathroom of a seedy hotel.' A briefing note reminds you that society now promotes two messages at once: that attacking a public figure is nearly impossible and the attacker becomes a despised pariah, versus that it is very easy and the attacker becomes the center of international attention.
assets.stage_1_question: Before you speak, which elements of Draft A are most likely to increase the risk of future attacks, and why?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The glamorizing details are the risk: the arsenal, the skilled-marksman persona, and the touch-and-go struggle attach a powerful, attractive persona to the criminal - the exact image that media-age assassins want, since, as Arthur Bremer wrote, they want 'a big shot and not a little fat noise.' Presenting the capture this way converts an identity-seeking failure into identity, which is the same social-proof dynamic that makes attacks cluster after wide publicity: the coverage says, 'You see; it can be done.' Getting caught for awful violence becomes the biggest day of one's life instead of the start of oblivion.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You must now refine the briefing and its optics for maximum de-escalation of future risk. Which package of presentation choices follows de Becker's recommendations for deflating the fantasy?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The debunking package: describe him as 'more of a loser, actually,' say he was found 'hiding in the bathroom - in the clothes hamper,' and note that 'he's never succeeded at anything else'; show the dirty underwear and socks on the bathroom floor rather than the bullets on the bureau; show him in a mangy T-shirt, handcuffed to a pipe, watched by one guard, and a woman at that; use the least glamorous incarnation of his name, calling him Ted Smith, known as Chubby Ted; and switch the focus to the people and methods that oppose assassins, commending the eight-man team of special agents whose work and new technologies made the apprehension possible. Not many identity-seeking would-be assassins would see those images and say that this is the life for them. The contrast case is the staging of Timothy McVeigh's arrest and the Ted Kaczynski coverage, where helicopters, agent escorts, and cover headlines calling the offender a genius promoted the glorious aspects of media crimes.
key_concepts: Society appears to be promoting two very different messages: attacks are nearly impossible and the attacker becomes a reviled pariah, versus attacks are easy and the attacker becomes the center of international attention.
Describing an arrest as a victory over a dangerous, powerful, well-armed and clever adversary attaches to the criminal a persona attractive to many who might consider undertaking a similar crime.

De Becker proposes casting the offender in a far less glamorous light: 'More of a loser, actually... We found him hiding in the bathroom - in the clothes hamper... He's never succeeded at anything else.'
De Becker recommends not showing the bullets on the bureau in the seedy hotel room but the dirty underwear and socks on the bathroom floor.
Getting caught for some awful violence should be the start of oblivion, not the biggest day of one's life.
Reporters usually refer to assassins with triple names like Mark David Chapman and Lee Harvey Oswald; those men were simply Mark, Lee, and Arthur.
De Becker suggests calling a criminal Ted Smith instead of Theodore Bryant Smith, or using a pre-attack nickname like Chubby Ted.
Guarded by federal agents, whisked into helicopters, and described as meticulous, the captured planner learns his coverage promotes the glorious aspects of assassination.

Timothy McVeigh's arrest was staged with a motorcade and a two-helicopter armada, and Ted Kaczynski appeared on the covers of TIME, U.S. News and World Report, and Newsweek twice, with cover text calling him a genius.
In 1911 criminologist Arthur MacDonald proposed that newspapers, magazines, and authors cease to publish the names of criminals, because the hope for glory is a great incentive to such crimes.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests social-proof contagion in threat communications: coverage of an attack or capture functions as advertising for the crime, raising or lowering the ability belief of other would-be attackers. De Becker's evidence is the observed clustering of attacks after publicity and his recommended de-glamorizing press posture, echoing criminologist Arthur MacDonald's 1911 proposal to stop publishing criminals' names.
